She quit the Gray Lady in 2020 , claiming censorious progressive activists were running amok @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ said she was bullied by colleagues who branded her " a Nazi and a racist " and complained whenever she was " writing about the Jews again " . Far from becoming a footnote in the history of modern American journalism , as her detractors reassured themselves she would , Weiss has gone on to found a burgeoning media empire . <p> Her flagship is The Free Press , a Substack-hosted news and commentary site with 1.25 million subscribers ( 155,000 of them paid ) and a reputation for ideological heterodoxy . Weiss has also found the time to become a podcaster , book author , debate moderator and co-founder of a private liberal arts college . <p> Progressives denounce the FP as an echo chamber for affluent ex-liberals who resent the Democrat Party 's leftwards shift , but its editorial line defies easy classification . It represents , depending on your view , either liberalism with its head screwed on or conservatism with a heart transplant . <p> FP readers are instinctively liberal but dismissive of radicalism . They love America and they like Israel . Their favourite senator @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ They are for free speech and open inquiry and believe the left has replaced the religious right as the chief enemy of both . <p> Unthinkingly post-racial , they are perplexed by progressive racialism , and while relaxed about God and gays they are sceptical of transgender ideology . If a New York Democrat fell into a coma in 1995 and reawakened in 2025 , he would be a Free Press subscriber before the week was out . <p> Weiss 's achievement is such that , according to Dylan Byers , Puck 's well-connected media correspondent , Paramount Skydance is in talks to buy the FP and hand Weiss a senior news role at CBS . None of the parties are confirming or denying but it would represent the sweetest revenge of all for Weiss . She 's the ultimate Jewish success story : she 's broigused her way to the top . <p> The legacy media that drove her out and then danced on her professional grave faces the prospect of her triumphant return , at a far higher level than she would likely have attained had they simply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the nest , this time with executive parking . <p> For media progressives , it would be especially wounding if Weiss took command of CBS , the network of Murrow , Sevareid and Cronkite . Paramount is poised to defile the temple of their idols , those gods behind the microphone who did real journalism , the kind that held the powerful to account -- provided they were somewhere to the right of Eugene McCarthy . <p> Hence the vituperation with which the reports have been met . Jack Mirkinson of The Nation calls Weiss " one of the leading hateful propagandists of our time " , who should be " dismissed as a crank and a bigot , and never heard from again " . The New Republic 's Michael Tomasky breathlessly predicts that CBS would soon be appealing to " wealthy people ... who , while not openly racist or sexist in most cases , nevertheless get the heebie-jeebies from all those Black and brown and trans people screaming about their rights . " Former Washington Post influencer Taylor Lorenz tweets : " The right wing grift economy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ CBS staff are " apoplectic " at the prospect of Weiss taking over , particularly with relation to the network 's coverage of the Israel-Hamas war . <p> While professional resentment no doubt plays some part in all this , it 's the reference to Gaza that gives the game away . This is mostly about ideological animus , both for Weiss personally and her journalistic ethic . They hate her because she is a traitor many times over . She 's a woman , a gay woman , and a gay Jewish woman . She is meant to be one of them . <p> They hate her journalism because it fails to reflect the personal prejudices of journalists and other graduate , urban , coastal progressives , who see in the humanitarian disaster in Gaza an opportunity to rid American politics and public opinion of its intergenerational sympathy for Israel . Now , they hope , when the boomers die off American Zionism will flatline with them . <p> The FP has been a dissenting voice from the American media 's coverage of the conflict , which grows more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in part a reflection of newsroom demographics . <p> Mainstream American journalists , and the journalism they produce , has long been more liberal than the median American . A 2022 study by Syracuse University found just 3.4 per cent of journalists surveyed identified as Republicans compared to 36.4 per cent for the Democrats . What has changed in the last decade or so is the abandonment of objectivity as a journalistic principle on the superstition that a surfeit of balance and impartiality is what brought about the rise of Donald Trump . <p> Objectivity must be abandoned to fight systemic racism , misinformation , climate scepticism , transphobia -- anything , really , that journalists decide to add to the list , which now includes Israel . This puts the profession at odds with the people who pay for it . While 76 per cent of Americans say journalists should give equal coverage to all sides of a story , only 44 per cent of American journalists agree . <p> That is why Bari Weiss infuriates them . @@129154679 <h> Not the 1930s , but the 1230s : How medieval blood libels returned to poison our age <p> Nazism was top-down , a state machine of propaganda and genocide . What we see now is older , more insidious : grassroots libels , spread by self-anointed authorities <p> September 10 , 2025 11:02 <p> Medieval blood libels have returned in modern form to poison our age ( Image : X ) <p> 4 min read <p> That London in 2025 requires a rally against antisemitism is shame enough . That it has had to be organised by Jewish groups and that the Labour government refused to send even a single representative only made matters worse . <p> The urgency is clear . A new survey shows antisemitism in Britain rising sharply . Particularly chilling is the growing number who now tell pollsters that Israel treats Palestinians " like the Nazis treated the Jews " . Such Holocaust inversion is doubly poisonous : it trivialises the Holocaust and retroactively justifies it by demonising Jews , accusing them of committing the very crimes they endured . Holocaust inversion turns Jew-hatred into @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ evidence that we are reliving the 1930s but rather the 1230s . Nazism was top-down : a state machine of propaganda and extermination . What we see now is older and more insidious . It is the medieval pattern revived : grassroots libels , spread by self-anointed authorities , rewarded by incentives , and eventually laundered into legitimacy when governments are pushed to echo them . <p> The parallels are disturbingly close . In the Middle Ages , the initiative usually came not from popes or kings but from local clerics and agitators . Illiterate populations relied on priests to tell them what to believe . Parish pulpits and monasteries turned rumour into revelation . Today , literacy is universal , yet the dynamic is the same . Today 's priests and agitators , our information gatekeepers , are NGOs , academics , journalists and UN rapporteurs . When they declare that Israel is " deliberately starving Gaza " or " committing genocide " , their followers believe it with the same fervour medieval congregants once brought to sermons about ritual murder . <p> And as then , so now @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ In Norwich or Trent , the tale was of Jews murdering Christian boys in secret rituals . Today the charge is that Israel deliberately kills children or starves infants . No claim is too fantastical , too gruesome , to go hysterically reported as fact . The most basic journalistic standards are routinely abandoned if the target is the Jewish state . We look back at those " primitive " centuries and wonder how people could have believed such nonsense as ritual slaughter . Yet in our own enlightened information age , almost identical charges are swallowed whole . <p> The incentives are also the same . Then , libels produced confiscated Jewish property , cancelled debts and pilgrimage revenues . Now they generate donations , grants , political leverage and attention . Outrage is a currency , and supply rises to meet demand . <p> So too the legal theatre . In Trent or Lincoln , Jews were dragged into courts where guilt was scripted in advance . Today , we have Corbyn 's Gaza tribunal , UN commissions , and Oxford show-debates : morality plays in legal , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the British government ? The problem is not that it lacks evidence to refute these libels but the will to use it . The work of dismantling many of the accusations thrown at the Jewish state has already been done . Scholars of " genocide studies " have been exposed as including activists masquerading as academics , twisting both law and fact . The IPC report has been credibly shown to have manipulated data and standards . Children allegedly starved by Israel and paraded for Western consumption have later been revealed to suffer from severe pre-existing conditions . Even Hamas 's own health ministry has not dared to claim the over 3,000 deaths from hunger that a genuine famine , as declared by the IPC in northern Gaza on August 22 , would by now have produced . It has facilitated peace talks between Israel and Hamas , did the same with the Taliban and the US during the war in Afghanistan , and hosts the Al Udeid air base , the largest American military base in the Middle East . <p> For decades the arrangement has held . @@129235577 <h> How can artists work with integrity amid global events ? <p> The arts have always responded to conflict . Whether through protest songs , resistance theatre , underground exhibitions or bold curatorial choices , cultural work often dares to speak when politics falls silent . But in these challenging times , that responsibility becomes heavier . The stakes are higher because art is not made in a vacuum . <p> When regimes change and when conflict may eventually end , another struggle begins : the one for justice . But what happens if , after everything we 've seen , justice is not served ? Many governments with the power to intervene in the genocide unfolding in Gaza have chosen instead to look away , prioritising geopolitical alliances . Despite overwhelming public outcry , there has been a global failure not only of leadership but also of values . <p> For those of us working in the arts , this raises the question : when conflict ends but accountability does n't come , how do we -- curators , artists , producers , audiences -- continue our work with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that is seemingly turning its back on justice ? <p> These questions do n't apply to Gaza alone . Consider other recent conflicts -- in Ukraine , the war continues with civilian lives shattered , infrastructure decimated and violations of international law being contested in courts and in the public consciousness . Around the world , state violence persists in regions less visible in Western media . The patterns of delay , denial and selective outrage repeat . <p> But this is n't new . History offers many examples that continue to shape how we think about justice , accountability and healing after times of deep division and trauma . In post-apartheid South Africa , the Truth and Reconciliation Commission gave a platform to victims and perpetrators alike . It was n't perfect , but it gave society a means to speak , to remember and , crucially , to heal . In Rwanda , after the 1994 genocide , the country turned to local Gacaca courts -- community-led processes rooted in traditional justice . In the aftermath of the Yugoslav wars , the International Criminal Tribunal for the former @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ survivors . These efforts were slow , flawed and often political -- but they acknowledged the pain . <p> At the recent International Society for the Performing Arts series in Edinburgh -- a joint programme between the ISPA and the Edinburgh Fringe Society -- Egyptian theatremaker and cultural leader Ahmed El Attar delivered a powerful speech . He reminded attendees that art does not exist outside of history and that cultural production -- especially in regions marked by occupation and conflict -- is inseparable from the politics that shape it . <p> If there is no justice , what does solidarity look like ? Can we , or should we , continue hosting artists from countries whose governments have been complicit in the suffering of others ? Can we justify international collaboration when accountability is absent ? <p> If we cancel cultural engagement entirely , we risk isolating the very people who are most in need of support <p> El Attar asked his audience to imagine , for a moment , that it was the 1940s . They had just witnessed the Holocaust . Would they have welcomed German artists @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collaborated with Italian creatives while fascist policies still lingered in the air ? These historical parallels are n't perfect , but they help us grasp the stakes of any post-conflict cultural reckoning . <p> Many of these artists are themselves survivors , dissidents and citizens caught in systems they may not support . Some are resisting , often quietly , under threat . Others are trying to tell stories that would otherwise be erased . The mistake would be to conflate governments with the individuals living and creating within them . <p> If we cancel cultural engagement entirely , we risk isolating the very people who are most in need of support . We risk abandoning the artists who are speaking out from inside oppressive regimes and leaving them as collateral damage in a global campaign for justice . <p> That 's the complexity . We must resist complicity but without turning resistance into abandonment . We must interrogate who we invite , but also ask why and what their work is really saying . This is about discernment , not blanket decisions . <p> Not all artists can speak @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And we must ensure they are not forgotten in cultural boycotts that can , inadvertently , silence dissent more than amplify it . <p> At the same time , programming today is no longer just about taste or innovation -- it is also about ethics . We will be judged on who we give platforms to , and why . Audiences are already asking the hard questions . We must be ready to answer them . Because when justice may be considered to fail in courts , it may still live in galleries , on stages , in songs and in scripts . However , if we do n't do the hard thinking now , it 's the silence that may speak louder than anything we could have said .

@@129244311 <h> King Bibi <p> Over three decades , Benjamin Netanyahu has shaped Israel in his own image <p> Why is Netanyahu so influential ? First elected as prime minister in 1996 , he has won five elections since , making him the longest-serving leader in Israel 's history ( exceeding even David Ben-Gurion , its founding PM ) . He has spent just 18 months out of office since 2009 . His right-wing politics , particularly his approach to the Palestinian question , have profoundly shaped Israeli society and public opinion . He has seldom been personally popular ( recent polls suggest only 40% of Israelis trust him ) , but " King Bibi " , an exceptionally shrewd operator , long ago established himself as " Mr Security " , the man best placed to protect Israel from its enemies , notably Hamas and Iran . <p> To his detractors , he is ruthless , reckless , a danger to democracy who prioritises his own political survival over Israel 's interests -- and , of course , the driving force behind the brutal war in Gaza . He is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Israeli politics today , and arguably in the entire Middle East.Where do his politics come from ? Not least , from his father . He was born in Tel Aviv in 1949 -- the middle son of Benzion Netanyahu , a Polish-born medieval historian who was a Revisionist Zionist ( militant , territorially maximalist ) and was often openly critical of his son . His teenage years were spent between Israel and Philadelphia , where his father taught ; but when he was 18 , in 1967 , he moved back to Israel for military service . <p> During five distinguished years in the army , he fought in Lebanon and served in the Sayeret Matkal , Israel 's equivalent of the SAS , alongside his brothers Yonatan and Iddo , to whom he was close . In 1976 , Yonatan ( Yoni ) was killed during a special forces raid on Uganda 's Entebbe Airport to free the 106 mostly Israeli hostages held by Palestinian and German terrorists . The only Israeli military casualty of the operation , Yoni is revered as a national hero ; his death inspired @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to Netanyahu , who was in Boston , studying at MIT , to break the news to his parents ; he later founded an anti-terrorism institute in Yoni 's memory , setting him on a path to politics . He was hired by Israel 's ambassador to the US in 1982 , became its representative to the UN in 1984 , and was elected to the Knesset , Israel 's parliament , in 1988 . Five years later , he became leader of Likud , Israel 's main right-wing party ; and in 1996 he beat Shimon Peres to become PM . His first term was troubled . Right-wingers were furious that he agreed to cede 80% of Hebron to Palestinian Authority control , among other concessions in the occupied West Bank ; the Left accused him of " killing the peace " , by undermining the 1993 Oslo Accords , of which he was a fierce , long-term critic . He lost the 1999 election.How did he make a comeback ? Netanyahu served as foreign minister and then finance minister in Ariel Sharon 's government , before resigning in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Gaza Strip . In 2009 , he was elected PM again . Migration to Israel of more than a million citizens of the former Soviet Union ( at least 10% of Israel 's whole population ) over the previous 20 years had led the country 's politics to take a more conservative , nationalistic turn -- reinforced by the collapse of the peace process , the Second Intifada ( 2000-2005 ) and rising Palestinian terrorism . By 2007 , Hamas had taken power in Gaza.What policies has he pursued ? A champion of free market economics who has nurtured hi-tech startups , he has also gained notoriety for trying to reshape Israel 's institutions . His attempts at media manipulation , allegedly offering deals in return for favourable coverage , have embroiled him in two criminal cases ; while his proposed " judicial reform " law is widely seen as an attempt to weaken the judiciary . On the Palestinian issue , Netanyahu , in theory , changed tack in 2009 , endorsing a two-state solution with a " demilitarised " Palestine . <p> But he continued to undermine it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ build on land in the West Bank designated by the UN as Palestinian . He has been in a coalition with ultra-nationalist settler parties since late 2022 . His Gaza strategy was , until recently , to keep Hamas in power , as a counterweight to the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank . He allowed Qatar to fund Hamas , believing that it could be safely contained militarily . Since Hamas 's attacks of 7 October 2023 , he has once again opposed a two-state solution , saying that he was " proud to have prevented the establishment of a Palestinian state ... after we saw the little Palestinian state in Gaza " . How did 7 October affect him ? The attacks , in which 1,195 people were killed and 251 taken hostage , were the result of serious intelligence failings , and initially dealt a crushing blow to Netanyahu 's reputation , and to his Hamas policy . His relentless prosecution of the war in Gaza since , in which 64,200 people have died , according to Palestinian authorities , has damaged Israel 's global standing ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It is widely suspected that he has kept the war going to delay a reckoning over his failures , and to reduce the possibility of his being tried on corruption charges , relating to media manipulation and allegedly receiving expensive gifts from businessmen.Why is he still in power ? What looked like a disaster has also proved an opportunity : it gave Israel the chance not just to destroy Hamas as a military force , but to decimate its ally Hezbollah in Lebanon , and to execute the " 12-day war " against Iran 's nuclear facilities . Netanyahu has seized the opportunity to redraw the map of the Middle East , humiliating Iran and its " axis of resistance " and bolstering his own position . @@129277613 <p> According to many of the riders , cycling should be separate from politics - the activists maintaining a right to protest as long as it 's nowhere near a bike . But , as Patrick Fletcher wrote in a feature from the 10 July 2025 issue of Cycling Weekly , bike races have long been the arena for protests . Subscribe to the magazine here . <p> Wind the clock back to 1982 , and you 'll find the Tour de France stopped in its tracks . <p> The location ? Denain , barely 10km from the start of the 2025 start line . The cause ? Steelworkers , hundreds of them , blocking the road in protest against the mass cuts that would effectively bring the Usinor plant to its knees . <p> It was the first and only time that a stage of the Tour de France was cancelled . There have been brief stoppages for various protests , stages curtailed or neutralised in extreme circumstances , and of course entire Tours cancelled during World Wars . But stage five of the 1982 Tour de France remains @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ race , of a stage abandoned altogether . That is a remarkable statistic , given the race 's high profile and the French penchant for protest . <p> Taking place over thousands of kilometres of public property , the Tour is almost uniquely vulnerable to sabotage . <p> Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsBy submitting your information you agree to the Terms &amp; Conditions and Privacy Policy and are aged 16 or over . <p> ( Image credit : L'Equipe ) <h> Steeled for action <p> Phil Anderson was easing himself into the yellow jersey as news broke on 6 July 1982 that 1,300 jobs would be lost at the Usinor steelworks in Denain . That was 90% of the workforce , already decimated from the 10,000-strong contingent of the 1960s . <p> " Usinor was the lifeblood of Denain , " said Jean Degros , a prominent local basketball player . " The announcement finished off the town . " <p> Running through the despair was a sense of betrayal , the Prime Minister @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ opposition but now , as they saw it , turning his back . <p> Stage five of the 1982 Tour was a team time trial , a scarcely believable 73km linking Orchies with Fontaine-au-Pire . Thirty kilometres from the finish line , the route would pass through Denain . It began as a crisis meeting , but the Tour presented an opportunity ; blocking the road was described in a L ' ? quipe report as an act of " collective spontaneity " . <p> The first team to set off were Splendor , the Belgian outfit of future world champion Claude Criquielion , leaving Orchies around 1pm . Tour de France boss Jacques Goddet was already in Denain , scrambling to muster a last-minute resolution . <p> He negotiated hard . According to local newspaper La Voix du Nord , Goddet offered to re-route the TTT through the Usinor plant itself in order to shine a spotlight on the workers ' plight . But it would n't do . Criquielion and his men reached the barricade and came to a halt . Slowly , the message filtered back and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ up , turn around and ride back to the start . Meanwhile , the huge crowds gathered at the finish in Fontaine-au-Pire wondered where the riders had got to . <p> It was a seismic moment . Goddet 's propensity to engage with the public - diplomatically making room for protest while keeping the show on the road - had contributed to his affectionate dubbing as ' the President of France for the month of July ' . As such , there was a sense of bewilderment as he addressed the television cameras in Denain : " To protest is natural , and the Tour de France can be a means to that end , but not to the point of impeding the race and stopping it , " he said , not so much angry as pained . <p> A line had been crossed , and nothing would be the same again . <p> ( Image credit : Getty Images ) <h> Held to ransom <p> Goddet 's style stands in contrast to the comparatively heavy-handed approach we see today . The current Tour chief Christian Prudhomme has made @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ any " ransom " demand rejected . Two protests stand out from recent memory . In 2018 , farmers - perhaps the race 's most consistent disruptors - lobbed hay bales into the road and were roundly pepper-sprayed by the police . Ironically , it was this response that actually halted the race as the lingering tear gas blew into the faces of the oncoming riders . <p> Three years ago , climate activists from Derni ? re Renovation temporarily stopped a stage by lying in the middle of the road in the shadow of a melting glacier . In truly remarkable scenes , the CEO of the race organiser ASO Yann Le Moenner took it upon himself to assist the police and forcibly start dragging protestors - in this case , two chained together by the neck-from the road . <p> Times are , of course , rather different . The Tour has continued to expand , and the increase in terror events in the 21st century has necessitated an entirely new , beefed-up security landscape . It was following the attacks in Paris in late 2015 and in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forces division - was deployed at the Tour for the first time in 2016 . It has remained ever since . <p> The potential for protest is greater than ever , stretching beyond local grievances to global political causes . The rise in climate activism - and more recently , the war on Gaza - have become major flashpoints , with the pro-Palestinian BDS Movement calling for " more peaceful protests than ever " at the Tour . Beyond the threat from steelworkers , these are the two most pressing issues that could disrupt the race 's smooth running this year . <p> Over the past decade , the security presence has been ramped up by around 25% . Now , the Tour de France route is secured by no fewer than 28,000 officers across France 's various law enforcement divisions , most notably the national police and the Gendarmerie , technically a branch of the military . That equates to eight officers for every kilometre . It 's impossible to fully seal off the Tour de France , but you can get pretty close . @@129300306 <p> The Oasis reunion . Nationalised healthcare . Sir David Attenborough . Bannau Brycheiniog . Highland tweed . Baked beans and Barbour coats . There are some things about Britain that are universally , undeniably great . But , let 's be honest , there are plenty of others -- income inequality , racist riots , crumbling schools and roads and fading institutions -- that are not . <p> If you listen to either side of our rancorous politics , Britain is broken . A state in a state . Yet another government , swept in last year on a swell of cautious optimism , is already being written off . The monarchy is mired in scandal and seemingly fading in relevance . If you believe the press , everyone from non-doms to NHS nurses is fleeing for sunnier , lower-tax climes . And yet , in so many ways , the UK is still the envy of the world . The Lionesses . Adolescence . Paddington Bear . Christopher Nolan . Love Island . Andy Murray ; Harry Styles . Charli XCX ; Central Cee . For all its flaws , Britain still draws people from every corner of the world -- sometimes even those willing to risk everything to reach it . <p> In the mid ' 90s , peak Britpop and the Spice Girls heralded the era of Cool Britannia . Thirty years on , it 's time for a reappraisal . With that in mind , we 've assembled a group of modern British icons -- from an Oscar winner to a Heartstopper , pop royalty to sporting legends -- to get their read on what Britain means in 2025 . The good and the bad . And as it turns out , even if we do n't always see eye-to-eye , there 's a lot we can agree on . <p> On Emma Thompson : Dress , necktie and boots by Givenchy . Tights by Falke . Jewellery by De Beers . <p> There are a lot of ways to identify as British . <p> Anthony Joshua : Do I identify as British ? Yeah , of course I do . <p> Andrew Garfield : I 'm American and I 'm British , and I feel very happy that I get to be both . <p> FKA Twigs : I feel British , but I have been raised by other places and other cultures . <p> Ambika Mod : I have Indian heritage , and that informs a lot about me and my life , but I have always really identified as British . I 've got a very British sense of humour . <p> Munroe Bergdorf : My dad 's Jamaican and my mum is white British , from Birmingham , both from working-class backgrounds . And yeah , I do feel British . I feel like it 's taken some time to take ownership over that . When you 're a child of an immigrant , you grow up feeling like this place is , like , tolerating you -- it 's a club that you 're not really in , like somehow you 've got through the door , but it 's just an accident , and you should n't really feel too comfortable . <p> Ian Wright : My parents are Jamaican , but I 'm English and British first . " I was dealing with a lot of those people who , because of the colour of your skin , do n't see you as English . Britain would n't be what it is without the contribution of immigrants and all the people who have been able to call Britain home . <p> Wright : Patriotism -- long live the King , the Queen ; " stiff upper lip " and all that sort of stuff . @@129344947 <p> Bringing together more than 300 activists from 44 countries , including Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg , the civilian flotilla is the largest maritime aid convoy to head for Gaza since Israel 's invasion of October 2023 . <h> Where does the word sumud come from ? <p> Palestinians have long resisted exclusion and erasure . In 1948 , during the Nakba ( the " catastrophe " ) , Zionist militias destroyed 530 Palestinian villages , killing 13,000 Palestinians and displacing 750,000 others . The events culminated in the unilateral declaration of Israel in May 1948 . <p> However , modern usage of sumud is usually traced to the aftermath of the 1967 Arab-Israeli war , when Israeli captured the West Bank , the Gaza Strip and Jerusalem , as well as Syria 's Golan Heights and Egypt 's Sinai Peninsula . <p> An estimated 300,000 Arab residents were displaced in a series of events often referred to as the Naksa ( " the setback " ) . <p> Palestinian protesters run from tear gas fired by Israeli forces during a demonstration against Israeli outposts on Palestinian land , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2021 ( AFP ) <p> The Israeli government then encouraged settlements on Palestinian land in the annexed areas , while also targeting the civil liberties of Palestinians residents . <p> Israel banned displaying the Palestinian flag or even its colours . The law was lifted during the Oslo Accords in 1993 , but partially brought back under far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir in January 2023 . <p> Meanwhile , sumud was adopted as a national symbol and promoted by the Palestine Liberation Organisation throughout the late 1960s and 1970s . <h> What are the symbols of sumud ? <p> Sumud is often symbolised by the olive tree , a historic crop for Palestinians and an important part of rural Palestinian life . <p> Palestinian olive trees have been attacked by Israeli forces and settlers for decades , intensifying after Israel annexed the West Bank and Gaza in 1967 . <p> Replanting olive trees is significant in Palestinian culture as an everyday act of sumud . <h> Are there different kinds of sumud ? <p> Some Palestinians distinguish between two types of sumud : static sumud and resistance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first focuses on the act of staying on Palestinian land amid Israeli occupation and settler incursions . <p> The second emphasises more dynamic acts of defiance against occupation , incorporating the non-violent forms of civil disobedience that are part of Palestinian resistance . <p> Palestinian demonstrators hold a Palestinian flag with a portrait of PLO leader Yasser Arafat as foam thrown by Israeli soldiers drops from a roof in Nablus , West Bank , in January 1988 ( AFP ) <p> During the Palestinian uprising from 1987 to 1993 , known as the First Intifada , acts of resistance associated with sumud included strikes , boycotts , demonstrations and non-payment of taxes . <h> How has sumud featured in art and literature ? <p> The concept of sumud is often associated with the work of Palestinian lawyer , human rights activist and writer Raja Shehadeh . <p> In Shehadeh 's diaries of West Bank life during the 1980s , sumud is presented as the " Third Way " of resisting Israeli oppression " between mute submission and blind hate " that involves neither violent resistance nor passive acceptance . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Sicily , in July 2025 ( AFP ) <p> Shehadeh wrote in The Third Way ( 1982 ) : " Sumud is watching your home turn into a prison . You choose to stay in that prison because it is your home and because you fear that if you leave , your jailer will not allow you to return . " <p> More contemporary notions of sumud go further . Examples include Sumud : A Palestinian Reader , an anthology from more than 300 contributors about Palestinian resistance . <p> As the book 's preface says , sumud " is , above all , a Palestinian cultural value of everyday perseverance in the face of Israeli occupation . <p> " Sumud is both a personal and collective commitment ; people determine their own lives , despite the environment of constant oppressions imposed upon them . " <h> What have flotilla organisers said about sumud ? <p> Flotilla spokesperson Saif Abukeshek told Middle East Eye 's Khaled Shalaby before setting sail that its name was inspired by Palestine 's history of resistance . <p> " We look at Palestinians who @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and under this phase of genocide for 22 months , and still resist , still remain on their land , and still wake up every day looking forward to a new day in life , " said Abukeshek . <p> " That is resilience . That is what sumud means . So for us to be able to fight all the challenges that we face , we need to have resilience , and to be inspired by the Palestinian people . " <p> Middle East Eye delivers independent and unrivalled coverage and analysis of the Middle East , North Africa and beyond . @@129351101 <h> Breadcrumb <h> Declaring war on the climate <p> Sir Keir Starmer , the British prime minister , visits BAE Scotstoun after the government announced a ? 10 billion agreement with Norway to build Type 26 frigates - the country 's biggest ever warship export deal . <p> Number 10 / Creative Commons 4.0 <p> Spending on the world 's militaries is climbing rapidly . A major new report shows how this surge is affecting carbon emissions . <p> The figure for the emissions increase from military expansion could be as high as 59 million tCO2e . <p> War is on the increase . From Ukraine to Gaza , and Sudan to Yemen , military action is creating devastation . <p> This drives -- and is being driven by -- massive increases in military spending . Since militaries are fossil fuel-hungry -- both directly and indirectly -- this is exacerbating the climate crisis . <p> Data on military carbon footprints is poor , so governments can avoid responsibility . A new report is shining much needed light on the subject . <p> Target <p> In 2024 , global military spending @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the year before , even once inflation is factored out . This is the highest level since at least the end of the Cold War -- and perhaps during it as well . <p> The United Nations has pointed out that this is similar to the total Gross Domestic Product ( GDP ) of all African nations -- and about 13 times the size of foreign aid provided by wealthier nations to the Global South . <p> Current trends mean this level of spending is set to rise even further in the coming years . <p> For example , during the summer , NATO -- the 32-nation military alliance led by the USA , and including the UK -- set a new spending target . <p> Its member nations committed to increase core military spending from the current average of two per cent of GDP to 3.5 per cent GDP with a further 1.5 per cent to be spent on additional ' security ' measures . <p> Reservoirs <p> NATO accounts for about 55 per cent of the world 's military spending , so this will represent a substantial increase @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will trigger further military spending increases in other parts of the world . <p> This spending is fuelling arms races , further increasing the risk of war , and diverting resources away from urgently needed efforts to tackle poverty , inequality , and the climate and nature emergencies . <p> But what will be the effect of these military spending rises on carbon emissions ? <p> Military equipment relies on supply-chains of high carbon materials such as steel , aluminium , and ' rare earth ' metals . Wars destroy carbon reservoirs , from oil and gas storage facilities to forests and wetlands . <p> Production <p> The global carbon footprint of the military including armed forces and their supply-chains , but not the impacts of war itself , is estimated to be about 5.5 per cent of global emissions . <p> The figure for the emissions increase from military expansion could be as high as 59 million tCO2e . <p> Military spending rises will increase these emissions . However , the exact relationship between military spending and military carbon emissions is highly complex and not easy to predict . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to increase military activity , leading to rises in fossil fuel use by combat planes or warships ? <p> Or will the funding be used to expand the numbers of military personnel , leading to rises in energy consumption at military bases , or the construction of new bases ? <p> Or will extra money be mainly directed towards expanding arms production , leading to higher energy consumption in industry or in the production of high carbon raw materials ? <p> Emissions <p> Extra carbon emissions in the supply-chain could occur outside the home nation , making them harder to track . Then there is also the issue of additional global heating effects due to non-CO2 emissions from aviation in the stratosphere . <p> These complexities have led to a burst of research activity attempting to understand and predict how carbon emissions vary with military spending levels . <p> A new review report -- written by myself and published by Scientists for Global Responsibility -- has assessed the findings of 11 studies from the past two years that have tried to estimate how military spending rises will impact carbon emissions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of $100 billion will lead to an increase in the military carbon footprint of approximately 32 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent ( tCO2e ) . <p> However , the uncertainty in that figure is high due to limited data on military emissions and the complexities described above . Thus , the figure for the emissions increase could be as high as 59 million tCO2e . <p> Reconstruction <p> Applying this analysis to a specific case , we found that the increase in NATO 's military spending over the five years , 2019-24 has led to an increase in its military carbon footprint of about 64 million tCO2e -- similar to the territorial emissions of Bahrain . <p> Furthermore , the planned increase to hit the 3.5 per cent GDP spending target is likely to lead to an additional rise of about 132 million tCO2e -- more than the territorial emissions of Chile . <p> It is important to note that these are single-year totals and so , if spending is maintained at higher levels as currently planned , there will be a major cumulative impact of emissions on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ extra spending by NATO above 2024 levels would add about 1,320 tCO2e -- equivalent to the annual emissions of the whole of Brazil . <p> And these estimates do not include emissions due to the impacts of war-fighting , such as destruction of carbon reservoirs or post-war reconstruction . <p> Abate <p> As mentioned , the uncertainty in these estimates is high . Hence , one key recommendation of the report is that measuring and reporting of direct and indirect military carbon emissions are greatly improved , so that the changes resulting from military spending rises can be adequately monitored . <p> However , despite the uncertainties , the research is unequivocal in highlighting that much stronger efforts are needed to reduce the military carbon footprint . <p> This is not a message that militaries and militaristic governments want to hear . Even when they accept that there is a problem , they favour efforts to develop ' greener ' weapons systems . <p> Putting aside the serious ethical conflicts associated with this path , there are huge technical obstacles . Civilian decarbonisation researchers point to several sectors which are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , trucking , iron and steel , aluminium , and synthetic chemicals . The military is -- in technological terms -- an amalgamation of these sectors , meaning that it is the hardest of the hard-to-abate sectors . <p> Peace <p> This emphasises the urgent need to prioritise peace-building efforts in global affairs . Much greater use of diplomacy , mediation , and trust-building are essential . <p> The importance of more arms control and disarmament measures is undeniable . One more hopeful finding from our report is that , when military spending is cut , emissions tend to fall at a faster rate than they grew , because the least energy-efficient technologies tend to be retired first . <p> But the latest assessment by leading climate scientists is bleak . They say that the Paris 1.5 ? C target will be breached within a few years without " immediate , transformative action ... to reduce emissions " . <p> It is extremely difficult to see how the current and planned military spending increases can be reconciled with the transformative action necessary to prevent dangerous climate change . @@129358804 <h> Time for Lib Dems to raise their game on the big stage <h> The political whirlwind offers Ed Davey 's party an opening but it must show more boldness <p> Lib Dems loathe him . But the political upheaval that Nigel Farage has prompted heralds a momentous chance for the party . The last election already sounded the death knell of the old two-party system . Reduced to just eight MPs in 2015 , the Lib Dems gained 72 members in July last year , a record haul in both quantity and quality . ( I was an unsuccessful contender . ) <p> Now , as the party heads to Bournemouth for its autumn conference , the potential is brighter still . With votes split between six contenders -- surging Reform , relaunched Greens , nascent " Jezbollah " leftists and the Lib Dems , as well as Labour and the Conservatives -- the first-past-the-post system can deliver startling results . Polarisation makes moderates more conspicuous : the Lib Dem leader , Sir Ed Davey , is according to some opinion polls the country 's most popular ( or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ down Kemi Badenoch 's neck , and with a couple of dozen gains would overtake the Tories in the next parliament . <p> This is a huge change for a party that for a century resembled a minor-league football club , run by dedicated supporters and enjoying at best sporadic success on the field . It must now compete seriously . The past year has been spent digging in . Many of the 2024 victories were unexpected . On arriving in Westminster , new members were told firmly their priority was to get re-elected . That has meant building local party organisations , sometimes from scratch , as well as learning to navigate parliamentary procedures to sort out constituents ' problems . <p> Door-knocking and local campaigning are not to be sniffed at . They spell success and can dispel the alienation that fuels populist rage . Badenoch 's comment that the Lib Dems are merely " good at fixing their church roof " is a " badge of honour " , Davey says . <p> But on a national stage featuring spectacular meltdowns and posturing loudmouths , centrist do-gooding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ here . Davey 's decision to boycott the dinner for the visiting US president chimed with many . He warns against a " Silicon Valley stitch-up " in the digital trade deal with the US , and has flatly accused Israel of genocide in Gaza . Better ties with Europe remain a crusading , even overriding , concern for Lib Dem stalwarts . That issue was the kiss of life during the Brexit turmoil . It 's lost some lustre since . <p> Advertisement <p> Davey 's personal crusade , fuelled by life with his 17-year-old disabled son , is a better deal for carers . Many activists want to attack from the left , automatically opposing every spending cut -- tempting given Labour 's austerity policies but not wholly credible . The party wants higher taxes on banks and tech giants . It has less to say on wealth creation . A belated rethink of economic policy is promised . One big opportunity would be to campaign for tax reform , simplifying and flattening taxes , abolishing loopholes that distort behaviour and dampen growth . Young voters yearn for a party ready to say publicly that the triple-lock pension ratchet ( racket , critics say ) is unsustainable . <p> But radicalism is risky . The party 's seats include just the sort of leafy , prosperous areas where land-value taxation ( a longstanding back-burner policy ) would bite hardest . Reliable votes from pensioners count for more than putative ones from youngsters . Grassroots campaigning easily turns into clogging nimbyism . Few Lib Dems want to grasp that nettle . <p> The easier ambition , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ work too . " The party lacks a think tank , not least because of fears that such a body might siphon away money from donors or start uncomfortable debates . Lib Dem policies are written by hobbyists and approved by the enthusiasts who attend party conference . The results can seem impractical or outdated : the party is still wedded to its 20-year-old opposition to ID cards . <p> A change of gear looms at Bournemouth . @@129362447 <p> The genocide ruling , opioid death stats , and a love-triangle teen drama <p> TODAY 'S BIG QUESTION <h> Gaza genocide : will UN ruling change anything ? <p> The finding by a United Nations commission of inquiry that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza has been described as a landmark moment , after more than 64,000 people have been killed in the occupied Palestinian territories in nearly two years of war . <p> The commission cited statements by Israeli leaders , and the pattern of conduct by Israeli forces , as evidence of " genocidal intent " , and said its latest report on the war was " the strongest and most authoritative UN finding to date " . Israel firmly denies accusations of genocide and insists it 's conducting the war in Gaza in self-defence and in accordance with international law . <p> What did the commentators say ? The findings will have a " profound impact " , wrote Paul Nuki in The Telegraph , and " increase the likelihood of global sanctions against Israel " . Lawyers representing groups pushing for sanctions now have an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ add to the growing condemnation of Israel 's conduct . And , while " not formally binding " , it could have a " strong persuasive value " in the ongoing case against Israel and its leaders in the International Court of Justice , said law expert Professor Triestino Mariniello . The court " can not ignore " the findings , which give " unprecedented legal and political weight to the charge of genocide in Gaza " , he told the Palestine Chronicle . <p> Many Western countries , including the UK , have said that only a court can rule on whether genocide has been committed , said Bel Trew in The Independent , but that outcome " could take years " . Some say it might take up to a decade for the International Court of Justice to rule . By then , there " wo n't be much of Gaza -- or its residents -- left " . <p> What next ? As Israel launches its ground offensive in Gaza City , the report is " validation " for Palestinians , said Malak Benslama-Dabdoub , a lecturer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The Conversation . " For international law , it is a test . " The verdict will either trigger " real accountability " , including sanctions , embargoes and prosecutions , " or it exposes the gap between lofty promises and political reality " . <p> THE EXPLAINER <h> The UK 's opioid crisis : why the stats do n't add up <p> The number of opioid-related deaths between 2011 and 2022 in England and Wales is more than 50% higher than previously thought , according to a new report . <p> The publication of new data , from King 's College London , has profound implications for both government and social understanding of drug issues . The UK 's underestimated opioid problem reflects a " serious drug-related-deaths crisis " , said lead author Dr Caroline Copeland . <p> Why were these deaths under-reported ? The Office for National Statistics does not have access to post-mortem reports or toxicology results , so it is reliant on the information provided by coroners on death certificates . <p> For the ONS to be able to record a drug death from a specific @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the death certificate -- something that does n't often happen , particularly if multiple drugs are present in the body . <p> The King 's College researchers were able to access information from coroners ' reports to compile more reliable data . <p> How many people are killed by opioids in the UK ? Opioids are a class of natural or synthetic drugs -- some available on prescription , many illegal -- that have a morphine-like , painkilling effect on the brain . They include heroin , fentanyl , codeine and oxycodone . The King 's College research estimates they were responsible for a total of 39,232 deaths in England and Wales in the 11-year range of its report , compared with just over 25,000 estimated by the ONS . <p> The National Records of Scotland collates its own official information north of the border . It receives " more detailed pathology reports , but differences in how deaths are reported across the UK make it difficult to compare " , said the BBC . <p> What can be done ? Governments around the world have been scratching their heads @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Nitazenes -- a new and potent type of synthetic opioid -- seem to be a leading cause of addiction and one of the " fastest-growing groups of new psychoactive substances " in the world , said The Independent . <p> Because nitazenes are concocted in labs , they can be altered easily . Producers can make an " entirely new product of similar potency " , which is not always subject to legal bans , said The Economist . <p> Ultimately , if governing bodies do not take further action , do not keep up to date with new variations or collate accurate statistics , efforts to tackle the opioid crisis could suffer " underfunding " , said the King 's College researchers . @@129383751 <p> Israel occupied the West Bank and Gaza -- thus occupying one million Palestinians -- in 1967 , in the aftermath of the Six-Day War . Now , there are approximately 6 million Palestinians in those territories , yet Israel has comprehensively rejected the " o " word and its political ramifications . This is not " occupied " , but " administered " territory . <p> This area can not be " occupied " , the state says , because it was not under Palestinian sovereignty to begin with . In fact , it is the Jewish biblical and ancestral homeland -- so how can a people occupy their own land ? It is therefore " disputed " , Israel has righteously explained -- no more than a temporary situation , protracted by the absence of an acceptable political settlement . <p> Decades came and went and then the " a " word appeared : apartheid . Israel , much of the world argued and accused , was effectively asserting a de facto apartheid regime . With the expansion of Jewish settlement , there were two ethno-national communities under @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . There were separate roads , separate and different laws , a separate legal system , an endless multitude of roadblocks and snap-checking and frequent Israeli incursions into Palestinian areas administered by the Palestinian Authority through the 1993 " Oslo Accords " . <p> Still , Israel vehemently and vociferously repudiated the use of the word " apartheid " . The result is the evocatively titled exhibition Nothing could have prepared us , everything could have prepared us , which draws on over 35 years of his vast archive of photography , video and prints . According to the artist , it is a project that aims to establish " what can be created in the moment of leaving " . <p> The exhibition 's title emerged from the Turner prize-winning artist 's personal reflection on his own life : " Much as I try to pre-empt or prepare for things , I am always finding myself out of control . Photographs from 2005 of the Russian army rehearsing a military parade in Moscow , a photograph of the US-Mexico border from 2004-05 , and an image of the border on the Gaza Strip from the early 2000s take on an eerie and unmissable significance , aided by the obvious benefits of hindsight . @@129398066 <p> This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today , and has been written by our American colleagues . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> Widespread online videos of the bloody assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and atrocities in Gaza are the final step in a morbid trajectory of real death on screen , writes Derek McArthur . <p> The most common thing you 'll hear from people who have seen the video of Charlie Kirk 's assassination is not to watch the video of Charlie Kirk 's assassination . <p> It spread rapidly on every platform , the gunshot to the conservative activist 's neck happening so swiftly in the video that many unsuspectingly saw it before they could even grasp what they were seeing and click away . <p> And it 's truly traumatising footage . The amount of blood that pours from his body is unimaginable . Reports an hour or two after the shooting had him as alive , but those who saw the footage knew he was gone . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ; it was a recognisable face . It is a specific kind of shock to see that happen to someone familiar . Kirk had been a prominent presence throughout the Donald Trump era , a common fixture of debates and right-wing media , and engaged in some powerful , high-profile political associations . <p> Now that familiarity has been transformed into a bloody act of violence witnessed by millions , over and over . A single , brutal clip on a loop . Freely hosted by every major social media platform , no searching required . <p> The internet was always the place to see a dead body . It provided a freedom to satiate our strange desire for the macabre . And it did n't have to hold back on any of the gory details . <h> Read more : <p> Before the internet , real death on the screen was restricted to gaudy underground VHS compilations and live televised misfortune , which was often subsequently compiled into said compilations . Infamous mondo horror films like 1978 's Faces of Death purported to show real footage of death , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ then , much of it was staged , with the real footage mainly consisting of medical autopsy footage and tragic scenes from the Holocaust , and other historical events . <p> When the internet arrived , the floodgates were open . Gory shock websites like rotten.com once received insane amounts of traffic , updating often with picture posts of the now expected autopsies , car crash victims , and tragic historical events . Rotten.com even claimed to have a picture of Princess Diana 's corpse that of course turned out to be fake , but not before it saw huge benefit from the mass interest and publicity surrounding her death . <h> Read more : <p> The reason why such things were created , and even enjoyed , is lost to time now , but the internet was once an experimental hotbed for stretching the limits of free expression , before its widespread corporatisation led to tech companies defining that for us . It 's far too simple of an explanation in hindsight to write off these sites as made by sickos for sickos . Given their ubiquity , popularity @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be terribly worrying if that were the case . <p> The header banner from the now defunct rotten.com shock website ( Image : rotten.com ) <p> Shock sites were exactly that , a means of delivering shock value . With the rise of online video , the screen started to look and feel much more like the real world . LiveLeak , a video site with the front of citizen journalism , made its name off footage of military strikes and the ISIS beheadings of British aid workers . <p> This platform , and others like it , represented a major shift . It was n't about being shocking anymore , it was about raw and unfiltered reality . A curious look into the horrors of the world that mainstream news could n't and would n't show . It satiated the strange desire for the macabre but could now claim a purpose of bearing witness to harsh truths , however exploitative it was . <p> Real death online was once something that had to be sought out , a case of curiosity killed the cat . Most who visited these @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of their stomachs , but it was , at the very least , their own decision to visit and watch . <h> Read more : <p> The Kirk assassination video and the endless videos of atrocities in Gaza signal a dystopian leap forward in quite a morbid trajectory . Even the option or ability to look away has disappeared , and we all now must carry the thoughts and burden of witnessing such traumatic events . <p> The sight of blood is unavoidable when we live in a culture where everything is recorded with phones , and that unfortunately also includes the inevitable spectre of death . The assassination of Kirk can spread on every major platform before any moderation occurs and plant its gory images into the zeitgeist , and there 's not much that an Online Safety Act can do about that . <p> Extreme violence is being normalised in our collective psyche from all of this ; the negative effects likely deep and not yet quite apparent . Our brains were n't designed to comprehend and sort the intense rush of information that social media and the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have that rush be the tragic sight of a fellow human being losing their life . <h> Useful Links <p> This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . But the knock-on effect is that sometimes they can overshadow similar dishes that come from other places . The British apple pie is not quite an underdog in this fight , but it 's certainly less celebrated than its cousin from across the pond . <h> Most popular <h> Who marches against Tommy Robinson ? <p> It took a while for apples to take hold in the US . Only crab apples were native to America , and they were small and sour -- no good for baking with . The early colonists of Jamestown brought apple seeds and cuttings with them , but those seeds took a while to turn into trees , and when they did bear fruit , it was mainly used for cider . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recorded recipe for the dish in the late 14th-century cookbook The Forme of Cury . Alongside apples , the recipe calls for figs , raisins , pears , good spices and saffron . It is enclosed in ' cofyn ' or coffin pastry , which was really a cooking vessel and not designed to be eaten ( you will be relieved to hear I am not recommending coffin pastry for our pie ) . <p> For me , one of the most distinctively British aspects of our apple pie is our preference for Bramley apples . The Bramley apple is a truly British phenomenon , cultivated almost exclusively here ( a handful of niche farms can be found around the world ) . Come September , you ca n't move for Bramley apples in the UK . Enormous , bulbous , acid green and dwarfing their eating apple cousins , they are extremely sharp when raw , but mellow when cooked into a tart sweetness , with a near-fluffy texture . <p> The earliest British apple pies would not , however , have been made from Bramleys . The first @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Ann Brailsford , in her garden in Southwell , Nottinghamshire , in 1809 . Ten years later , Henry Merryweather , who owned a local nursery , took cuttings from the tree and grafted them on to rootstock to grow trees to sell . He named the apples they produced after Bramley the butcher . In 1900 , violent storms caused the original tree to fall , but it survived and is still bearing fruit today , more than 200 years since it was planted . <p> In an apple pie , Bramley apples will soften , while still holding their shape -- it is best to pile them @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ dip in the middle as the apples collapse . <p> It 's not just the Bramley apple that defines the British apple pie , though -- after all , in those early pies , Pippins were generally the preferred cultivar . We also take a different approach with the pastry , the spicing and the finish . Where America favours a thick , flaky pastry , often with a latticed top and sky-high chunks of eating apple , all tossed in cinnamon , our version is a little different . <p> We use shortcrust pastry , rolled thinly , undulating over the contours of the apples beneath , and then painted with egg white before caster sugar is scattered with wild abandon over the top . The warmth of cinnamon and nutmeg , cloves and mace are integral to a good apple pie , and I like the dance of the mixture of spices ; autumn fruit can stand up to strong spicing . <p> When it comes to serving apple pie , I am both an equal opportunist and capricious . Add cold water a spoonful at a time , squeezing the mixture to bring it together into a dough ; you should n't need more than about three tablespoons of water , and may get away with less . Wrap the pastry in clingfilm and refrigerate for at least half an hour . <p> Peel and core the apples , chop them into chunks about an inch and a half wide , and toss them in the lemon juice in a bowl . Add the light brown sugar and spice and toss again . <p> Preheat the oven to 200 ? C. Divide the chilled pastry into two parts , roughly two-thirds and one-third . Roll out the larger piece and lay it into the bottom of a pie dish , with some overhang at the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and then roll out and lay the smaller piece of pastry on top , completely covering the apples . <p> Crimp the edges of the pastry , or trim them and press them together with the tines of a fork . Cut two slashes in the centre of the pie to act as steam vents . Paint the pastry with egg white , and scatter the caster sugar on top . <p> Bake for 30-40 minutes , until the pastry is golden brown , and then leave to sit for 15 minutes before serving . <p> To sign up for Olivia Potts 's newsletter , which brings together the best of The Spectator 's food and drink writing , go to **31;305;TOOLONG <h> The secrets of a British apple pie <h> Read next <p> Israel 's operation to conquer Gaza city is now entering its third day . @@129400912 <p> On September 9 , a missile slammed into Doha . Israel claimed it was targeting Hamas figures . But the implications go far beyond a single strike . For the first time in decades , a Gulf capital -- long considered politically sacrosanct even amid wars in Gaza , Lebanon , Syria , and Yemen -- was pulled directly into the conflict . <p> The shock was immediate : an Arab-Islamic emergency summit convened , the UN scheduled a special debate , and markets began to price in new risks . <p> History turns on moments when the rules change . The Israeli strike in Doha was such a moment . It shattered the tacit understanding that Gulf capitals are off-limits , redrawing the map of vulnerability in the Middle East . What happens next will reverberate not only through the Gulf , but across energy markets , global trade and the fragile web of normalisation efforts linking Israel and its neighbours . <p> The Doha strike is more than a tactical episode in Israel 's long war with Hamas . It is a strategic inflexion point . It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Gulf , for Oman , and for the wider world ? Who stands to gain , and who stands to lose ? And how should policymakers chart a course through what looks like an era of mounting instability ? <p> The strike represents a new phase in the Middle Eastern conflict . Until now , Gulf capitals were treated as off-limits , even when regional wars escalated . By hitting Doha , Israel has expanded the battlefield . This shift forces GCC states to rethink the vulnerability of their own diplomatic , financial , and aviation hubs . The cost of protecting these hubs against drones , missiles , and cyberattacks -- will only grow . <p> The attack also undermines one of the region 's most fragile political projects : normalisation with Israel . While diplomatic channels may remain open , the political space for economic , technological , and security cooperation has narrowed . Quiet partnerships -- already sensitive -- have become politically costlier to sustain . <p> The economic consequences are immediate and global . The Middle East controls three maritime chokepoints -- the Suez Canal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- that carry a significant portion of global energy and trade . These routes were already strained by Ansar Allah-linked disruptions in the Red Sea . The strike on Doha adds another layer of geopolitical fragility . <p> Insurers are repricing risk . Some shippers are rerouting vessels around the Cape of Good Hope , extending transit times and increasing costs . Even minor disruptions can add a risk premium of two to five dollars per barrel of oil . <p> For Europe , this means higher imported inflation at a time when energy costs are already politically toxic . For Asia , it means delays and surcharges in supply chains that fuel its manufacturing economies . For emerging markets , it means capital outflows and tighter financial conditions as investors retreat at the first sign of Middle East volatility . <p> Oman , like its neighbours , sits at the centre of this shifting geography . Its neutrality and reputation as a convening power may increase in value . Salalah , Duqm , and Sohar ports could serve as alternative gateways if Red Sea or Gulf routes are further @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resilience and narrative discipline to maintain confidence among investors , shippers , and partners . <p> Three layers of action are needed for the region , and Oman in particular , to respond . <p> In the short term , the priority is de-escalation and protection . @@129422697 <h> What tripping in the countryside can tell you about Britain <p> Man on the radio asks if the countryside is racist . The English countryside . Is it racist ? Wild question . The permanent headquarters in New York City opened in 1952 and the organisation has other offices in Geneva , Vienna and Nairobi . <p> In spite of my criticisms about its overall effectiveness , the UN is essential to advance the goals of peace , sustainable development and human rights . <p> It still aims to work with member states to end conflicts and to forge sustainable peace . <p> The UN documents human rights violations , advocates for robust human rights protections and pushes for compliance with international laws and standards . <p> Aiming to achieve these goals is , of course , not the same as success . It follows the Global Development Initiative , the Global Security Initiative , and the Global Civilisation Initiative . <p> The GGI is a vital signpost for the UN of where the global majority wants to see it located . <p> It is more than a lone-wolf proposal from China . It is the articulation of discussions that have been taking place across the global South for years . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ without dismantling existing institutions . <p> Xi has made it clear that the aim is to improve the system 's inclusivity and fairness while addressing the major challenges of our time . <p> The Chinese leader pointed to the continued poison of cold war thinking , hegemonism , protectionism and new forms of instability . <p> The GGI has five key principles . <p> The first is sovereign equality . All countries , regardless of their size , economy or military capacity , should participate in global governance as equal partners . <p> Each nation has the right to determine its own social and political system without outside interference . <p> The second calls for respect for international law based on the UN Charter . <p> The third principle is that much talked about multilateralism . The world no longer wants to see poles of power or hegemonic rule . <p> Xi called for the joint management of global affairs and rejection of unilateralism . He insists the UN should remain the central body of international governance . <p> The fourth is a people-centred approach . Governance , he argued @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and sustainable development of people across the world rather than power competition . <p> The fifth principle is action not words . Xi said nations should work to deliver real solutions to real problems . <p> Xi 's insistence on the continuing importance of the UN is an important emphasis and , to be honest , has been tough for me to fully appreciate given its complete inaction on issues such as the genocide in Gaza and its sometimes complicity in US imperialism . <p> The UN , its charter and a number of other institutions , such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank , were created in the aftermath of the victory over Nazism , fascism and imperialism in World War II . <p> The UN was created to entrench the power of the US and its allies against the Soviet Union through its dominance of its most important body , the security council . <p> The council has five permanent members -- China , France , Russia , Britain and the US . @@129464592 <h> Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory : With UN deadline expired , all states must act <p> Ending the genocide is not enough . The illegal occupation must also be terminated <p> A convoy of Israeli tanks near the Gaza Strip on 16 September 2025 ( Menahem Kahana/AFP ) <p> On Thursday , a deadline set by the UN General Assembly for Israel to terminate its occupation of the Palestinian Gaza Strip and the West Bank , including East Jerusalem , expired . <p> It was set a year earlier , after the landmark 2024 advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ) , which affirmed a profound shift in approach to the question of the legality of the occupation . <p> The court ruled that the Israeli occupation is illegal not only in its conduct , but also in its very existence . It violates both the legal right of self-determination of the Palestinian people , and the legal prohibition on the acquisition of territory by force . <p> As a result , the ICJ noted , it must end as rapidly as possible . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ year to comply with the duty to withdraw . <p> But as that deadline expires , the occupation is even more entrenched and abusive , amid a genocide in Gaza , expansions in settlements and settler violence in the West Bank , and Israeli plans to declare the annexation of more territory beyond East Jerusalem . <h> New MEE newsletter : Jerusalem Dispatch <h> Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine , alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters <p> However , the court and the UN General Assembly did not only address Israel . They also affirmed the special legal obligations of all other states to suppress Israel 's violations of international law in maintaining the occupation . <p> These obligations are entirely separate from the duties they also have to suppress Israel 's discriminatory , abusive and genocidal treatment of the Palestinian people . They are also more fundamental and wide ranging , since they concern the occupation in and of itself , as a general matter . <h> What states must do <p> Legally , states must do three things . First , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the occupation to an end . This requires full-spectrum sanctions against Israel , and against individual Israelis . <p> Second , they must not recognise the occupation as lawful . <p> And third , they must not aid or assist Israel in maintaining the occupation . <p> The links between the Israeli presence in the occupied Palestinian territory , on the one hand , and so-called Israel proper , on the other - economic , societal , military , tourism , educational , cultural and more - are multifaceted and inextricable . It is thus impossible to disaggregate relations with the Israeli state and Israeli private actors to identify discrete matters not linked to the occupation . <p> Consequently , implementing the suppression obligations requires states to address Israel as a general matter . <p> In terms of arms and intelligence sharing , states must not provide any support to Israel whatsoever . It is not enough only to halt support that might be used to commit serious violations of the legal rules regulating the conduct of the occupation - such as torture , apartheid , grave breaches of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ since any and all support provided to Israel props up the existence of the occupation , one way or another . <p> Likewise , given the inextricable links between the economic dimensions of Israel 's presence in the occupied Palestinian territory and the Israeli economy more generally , states must adopt a total trade embargo against Israel - including , but not limited to , an embargo on settlement products . <p> Despite last year 's ICJ ruling and its endorsement by the UN General Assembly , many states still behave seemingly in denial of these fundamental legal issues : both the existential illegality of the occupation , and what that means for their behaviour . <p> Even the current focus on the Gaza genocide - while vital - if conducted in isolation from the bigger picture , ignores the fact that even without Israel 's ongoing legal breaches in its conduct of the occupation , its very presence as an occupier would still be a fundamental breach in and of itself . States would thus still bear the legal duty to bring this presence to an end . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Instead of criticising as illegal certain conduct only ( such as the lack of adequate aid provision in Gaza , or settlement expansion , settler violence and home demolitions in the West Bank ) , states must also criticise as illegal the occupation itself . <p> It is not enough to insist that Israel is not sovereign in , and can not claim sovereignty over , Gaza and the West Bank , including East Jerusalem . States must also not recognise as valid any other justifications Israel might make for its presence in any part of this Palestinian territory , including the assertion of self-defence . Any state accepting that Israel has a right to be present there on the basis of a right to self-defence breaches the duty of non-recognition . <p> The time is long overdue for all states to face up to the exceptional character of Israel 's violations of fundamental legal obligations in maintaining its presence in the occupied Palestinian territory - and the exceptional legal duty they have to suppress these violations . <p> Legally , they are not disinterested bystanders , free to pick @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ illegality of Israel 's presence . They are required to act , and to do so comprehensively . There is an urgent legal duty to depart from partial , selective and symbolic gestures and statements , to concrete , effective and all-encompassing action . <p> The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye . <p> Ralph Wilde is Professor of International Law at University College London , University of London .
